goldens.comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:214 — Selecting `resourceStore.findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId())` and consulting the `Clients` resource only when it is absent makes any object-scoped policy shadow the realm-wide grant promised by the evaluator contract, so an administrator with global manage/map-roles plus an unrelated per-client policy loses authority for that client (P1; confidence: high; delete only if object grants are explicitly override semantics rather than additive grants).

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real logic issue in hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope). The code first checks for a client-specific resource, and only if null does it check the realm-wide 'all-clients' resource. This means if a client-specific resource exists (even with unrelated policies), the realm-wide permission is never evaluated. Looking at the diff at lines 213-227, the logic is: find client-specific resource -> if null, check all-clients resource -> evaluate. This ordering means realm-wide grants are shadowed when any client-specific resource exists, which contradicts the expected additive permission model where having global manage should work regardless of per-client policies.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/ClientPermissionsV2.java:193 — Returning this evaluator from `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` while its interface method is a `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")` leaves the V2 implementation non-substitutable for the management lifecycle contract, coupling every caller to an undocumented feature-version check (P1; confidence: high; delete only if these inherited operations are formally removed from the V2 contract and the accessor cannot expose them).

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows ClientPermissionsV2 extends ClientPermissions and overrides several methods to throw UnsupportedOperationException (lines 155-195), including isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, getPermissions, etc. MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returns this ClientPermissionsV2 instance (lines 63-67). The interface ClientPermissionEvaluator declares these methods, so callers using the interface contract would encounter runtime exceptions. This is a legitimate architectural concern - the V2 implementation breaks Liskov Substitution Principle by throwing exceptions for inherited interface methods. However, this appears to be intentional design for a feature-flagged V2 implementation, and the finding correctly identifies a real coupling issue that requires callers to know which version they're using.

adjudication_records.issue_text: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/services/resources/admin/permissions/AdminPermissions.java:77 [P2, confidence: 78%] — Wrapping the pre-existing deletion cleanup in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` is untraceable to adding the Clients schema and means a client, role, or group deleted after that feature is disabled leaves its persisted authorization resources/policies orphaned rather than invoking the former unconditional `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)` cleanup.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the event listener code in AdminPermissions.java now wraps all cleanup logic (for RoleRemovedEvent, ClientRemovedEvent, GroupRemovedEvent) inside `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`. Previously, this cleanup was unconditional. This means if the feature is disabled after being enabled, deleting a client/role/group will no longer call `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)`, leaving orphaned authorization resources/policies in the database. This is a real behavioral change that could cause data inconsistency.

adjudication_records.issue_text: server-spi-private/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/AdminPermissionsSchema.java:101 — [P1][confidence: high] `resourceStore.findByName(resourceServer, name)` ignores the newly added resource type, so a client created or imported with the same ID as an existing user reuses that user's resource and overlapping `manage`/`view` grants, allowing a user-scoped administrator to manage that client and obtain or rotate its secret.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that resourceStore.findByName ignores the newly added resource type, causing client/user ID collisions. However, looking at the diff, the getOrCreateResource method at line 90+ shows that resources are looked up by name AND resourceType is used to determine how to resolve the name (resolveUser vs resolveClient). The resource names are resolved to actual entity IDs (user.getId() or client.getId()), and resources are created with the resourceType included. The findByName call uses the resolved name (entity ID) which would be different UUIDs for users vs clients. The finding misreads how the resource lookup and creation works - there's no evidence in the diff that client and user resources would collide or share permissions inappropriately.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/base/src/test/java/org/keycloak/tests/admin/authz/fgap/PermissionClientTest.java:359 — [P2, confidence: 96%] The single combined grant `Set.of(MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, CONFIGURE)` lets both succeeding role-mapping calls pass if any one of those newly introduced scopes is incorrectly accepted for either operation, so the test cannot detect a swapped or overly broad scope check.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test design weakness. In testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient(), a single permission is created with Set.of(MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE, CONFIGURE), then two operations are tested: adding client roles to a user and adding composite roles. Because all three scopes are granted together, the test cannot verify that each operation requires its specific scope (MAP_ROLES vs MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE). If the implementation incorrectly accepted MAP_ROLES for composite operations or vice versa, this test would still pass. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added permission logic, though not a bug in the production code itself.
